text:
HALLOWEEN 2026 · SATURDAY, OCTOBER 31
 Is your store ready for the weekend, or will a hidden problem scare your customers away?



 

 
 Summary
 Halloween lands on a Saturday this year, and any traffic spike is when hidden website problems cost the most. A weak offer is rarely why a store loses sales. Five hidden problems do far more damage.
 These are a checkout that throws an error, a page that crawls, and a phone layout that fights the shopper. The other two are a payment that fails for no clear reason and an order for stock you lack.
 Each section shows what the customer sees and how to confirm the cause with tools you already have. It also says when the fix is bigger than a settings change.


 

 
 Introduction
 The ecommerce website problems that cost the most sales are checkout errors, slow pages, and clumsy mobile buying. Payment failures and stock or integration data that does not match reality complete the list. Each one has a symptom shoppers notice and a fix.
 You can usually confirm the cause in an hour or two. Halloween is a fair excuse to go looking. This year it falls on a Saturday, so shoppers have a whole weekend to browse and buy.
 Seasonal promotions send extra traffic to your store. That traffic lands on the same checkout, product pages and payment setup as everyone else's, right before the holiday rush. The scariest problems are the ones you cannot see.
 Shoppers rarely report them. They just leave.
 Most advice on this topic tells you what to improve. This guide is about diagnosis: something is going wrong, so how do you find out what? It works on any platform, with WooCommerce examples where the steps are platform specific.
 Design and usability problems are a separate topic.

 Which ecommerce website problems should you check first?
 Start with the problems that stop a sale outright. A broken checkout or a failing payment loses every shopper who hits it. A slow page only loses some of them.
 This table is the short version of the five sections below. Use it to jump to the one that matches what you are seeing.
 Problem What the customer sees First check Usual fix 
 Checkout will not complete Button does nothing, no shipping options, valid address rejected Browser console and shipping zones Remove the script conflict or repair the shipping rule 
 Slow pages Blank spaces, images popping in, laggy taps Field data in Search Console and PageSpeed Insights Images, scripts, caching or hosting, depending on the report 
 Mobile frustration Tiny buttons, covered content, stacked pop-ups Buy something on a real phone Larger tap targets, fewer pop-ups, simpler variation pickers 
 Payment failures Payment failed, or charged with no order Order notes, WooCommerce logs and the gateway dashboard Keys, webhooks, firewall rules or a plugin fix 
 Wrong stock and orders Sold out after payment, wrong item, odd shipping cost Compare stock in every system Faster sync, error alerts and clean data mapping 
 


 

 
 What should you check before Halloween weekend?

 Fifteen minutes now is cheaper than a lost weekend of sales. Run one quick check for each nightmare, on a phone, before the traffic arrives. The same list works before any promotion.
 Checkout: place a guest test order with an address outside your usual shipping zone.
 Speed: run your top category page and best-selling product page through PageSpeed Insights and read the real-visitor data first.
 Mobile: tap through a product page and the cart on a real phone with your cookie banner and pop-ups showing.
 Payments: scan recent failed orders and your gateway dashboard for clusters of the same error.
 Stock: compare the ten best sellers, and anything on promotion, against your warehouse or ERP.
 Fix what you can before the weekend. Leave bigger changes until it is over, and use the sections below when something fails.


 

 
 NIGHTMARE 1 OF 5 · CHECKOUT
 Nightmare 1: Why can't customers finish checkout?
 Usually because something on the page broke, not because the shopper changed their mind. The usual suspects are a script error or a shipping rule that returns no rates. Others are a field that rejects valid input or a cached page showing stale data.
 What the customer sees
 The Place order button spins and nothing happens. The page says no shipping options are available. A valid address gets rejected.
 The total changes between steps. From the shopper's side the store looks broken. Nobody wants to hand a card to a broken store.
 Why it matters
 Checkout is the last step, so every failure here costs a sale from someone who had already decided to buy. These problems also hide well.
 Your own test orders work because your address sits inside the shipping zone you set up. Your browser also has no conflicting extensions.
 Likely causes
 Shipping setup: an address outside every shipping zone or products with no weight or dimensions. Without them a rate calculator cannot quote. Another cause is a carrier plugin that times out.
 Validation rules: postcode, phone or state fields that reject real formats. Examples are apartment addresses, Canadian postcodes and phone numbers with extensions.
 Script conflicts: a chat widget, pop-up tool or speed plugin that combines or delays JavaScript. It can stop the checkout button from working, often right after an update.
 Caching: cart, checkout and account pages served from cache, which shows stale totals.
 Security rules: a firewall or security plugin that blocks the request that submits the order.
 How to confirm it
 Place a test order in a private browser window, as a guest. Use three addresses. Pick one far from your warehouse, one with an apartment number, and one in another country you ship to.
 Open the browser developer tools (press F12), go to the Console tab and click Place order. Red errors point to a script conflict.
 Switch to the Network tab and look for a request with a red status such as 403 or 500. A 403 often means a firewall or security rule is blocking it. A 500 means the server hit an error, so check WooCommerce, then Status, then Logs.
 Compare dates. If checkout completions dropped on a particular day in your analytics, check what changed that day. Common culprits are a plugin update, a theme change or a new script.
 On a staging copy, switch plugins off in small groups and retest until the clash disappears. Do not do this on the live store.
 How to fix it
 Add a catch-all shipping zone and require weights on shippable products. Loosen validation so it accepts real-world formats. Exclude cart and checkout from JavaScript combining, delay settings and page caching.
 Replace or reconfigure the conflicting plugin, then retest with the same three addresses. If checkout still fails after those checks, consider professional WooCommerce checkout repair .


 

 
 NIGHTMARE 2 OF 5 · SPEED
 Nightmare 2: Why do slow pages drive shoppers away?
 Because a page that is slow to show its main image or respond to a tap feels broken. A shopper with other tabs open will not wait to find out.
 What the customer sees
 Grey boxes where products should be. Images that appear one at a time. A filter that takes a second to react, and a layout that jumps just as the shopper goes to tap.
 Why it matters
 Product and category pages are where shoppers choose what to buy. Google also measures this on real visits, using Core Web Vitals .
 Google rates the main content as fast when it loads within 2.5 seconds. It says the same for an Interaction to Next Paint of 200 milliseconds or less.
 Likely causes
 Large, uncompressed images, especially hero banners and product galleries.
 Third-party scripts: chat, reviews, heat maps, tracking tags and pop-ups that load on every page.
 Page caching that is missing or set up wrongly.
 Slow server response from an under-sized hosting plan.
 A heavy theme or page builder that ships far more code than the page needs.
 Plugin database queries, such as filters, related-product widgets and search tools, that run on every category page.
 How to confirm it
 Check real-visitor data first. In Google Search Console, open the Core Web Vitals report. In PageSpeed Insights, read the field data at the top before the lab score. Lab scores can swing from one run to the next.
 Test the pages that make money. Those are a category page, your best-selling product page and the cart, not only the home page.
 Read what the report blames. A high server response time points to hosting, caching or slow database work. A large image flagged as the Largest Contentful Paint element points to image size or format. A long list of unused JavaScript points to plugins and third-party tags.
 Open developer tools, go to the Network tab, reload the page and sort by size, then by time. The heaviest file and the slowest request are usually easy to spot.
 On WordPress, a free plugin such as Query Monitor shows slow database queries and which plugin is running them.
 How to fix it
 Match the fix to the finding. Resize and compress the biggest images. Remove tags you no longer use.
 Turn on page caching, but not for cart and checkout. Ask your host about server response if that was the flagged item. Measure again after each change so you know what worked.
 Store-specific steps for WooCommerce are covered in WooCommerce speed without switching hosts . If you would rather hand it over, Virtina offers ecommerce performance optimization .


 

 
 NIGHTMARE 3 OF 5 · MOBILE
 Nightmare 3: Why does a responsive store still feel bad on a phone?
 Because responsive only means the layout fits the screen. Mobile-friendly means a person can actually buy something with one thumb, on a slow connection, while distracted.
 What the customer sees
 Links too close together to tap accurately. A sticky header and cookie bar that cover a third of the screen. Size and colour pickers that need three attempts.
 A pop-up whose close button sits off screen. A keyboard that hides the field being typed in.
 Why it matters
 Plenty of shoppers browse and buy on phones, so a clumsy experience is not a niche problem. It also hides in your numbers. Low mobile conversion gets explained away as shoppers just browsing, when the page itself is often the cause.
 Likely causes
 A desktop design squeezed onto a small screen instead of designed for thumbs.
 Variation selectors, such as dropdowns and tiny swatches, built for a mouse pointer.
 Stacked overlays: cookie banner, newsletter pop-up, chat bubble and discount bar all at once.
 Sticky elements that take too much of the viewport.
 Pages that are too heavy for a mobile network.
 How to confirm it
 Complete a purchase on a real mid-range phone on mobile data, and time it. Browser device mode is useful for checking layout, but it cannot reproduce thumb reach or a slow network.
 In GA4, compare add-to-cart and conversion rates for mobile and desktop. A large gap at one step shows where to look.
 Watch ten mobile session recordings in a tool such as Microsoft Clarity or Hotjar. Look for repeated taps on things that do not respond.
 How to fix it
 Make tap targets roughly 44 to 48 pixels with space between them. Allow one pop-up at most, delayed, with a large close button. Turn variation choices into big buttons instead of small dropdowns.
 Shrink or remove sticky bars. Wallet buttons and buy now pay later are covered in WooCommerce mobile checkout .


 

 
 NIGHTMARE 4 OF 5 · PAYMENTS
 Nightmare 4: How do you tell a payment failure from a legitimate decline?
 Look at the pattern. A legitimate decline belongs to one card or one customer and carries a reason from the bank. A technical failure hits many customers at once.
 It often shows an error from your own setup instead of a bank reason. It tends to start right after a change.
 What the customer sees
 The payment fails with a vague message. A wallet button errors out. A 3-D Secure window opens and never returns.
 Worst of all, the customer is charged but the order shows as failed or pending. They have to email you to find out what happened.
 Why it matters
 A real decline is the bank doing its job, and you cannot fix it. A technical failure is yours to fix, and it keeps costing sales until someone notices. The trouble is that both look like payment failed in your order list.
 Likely causes
 Configuration: expired or changed API keys, test mode left on, or a webhook address or secret that no longer matches.
 Blocked callbacks: a firewall, security plugin or host rule that stops the gateway from reporting back. Paid orders then stay on Pending payment.
 Authentication steps: 3-D Secure or wallet flows that fail. A script conflict, pop-up blocker or redirect problem stops the shopper returning to your store.
 Plugin conflicts and outdated payment plugins after a WooCommerce or PHP update.
 Over-strict fraud rules, in the gateway or in a plugin, that reject genuine customers.
 How to confirm it
 Open a failed order and read the order notes. WooCommerce usually records what the gateway returned.
 Go to WooCommerce, then Status, then Logs, and open the log for your payment gateway. Look for repeated errors with the same message.
 Open the gateway's own dashboard and compare. Declines with a bank reason, spread across different customers, are normal. A cluster of API or authentication errors is not.
 Check timing. Did the failures start after an update, a key change or a plugin install?
 Look for paid orders stuck on Pending payment. If the gateway shows success and your store does not, the callback is not reaching you.
 Place a test order using the gateway's test mode, on a phone and on a desktop.
 This table gives you a quick way to read what you find.
 Signal Usually a legitimate decline Usually a technical failure 
 Who is affected One card or one customer Many customers across different cards 
 Message A bank reason, such as insufficient funds or card declined An API, authentication, key or webhook error 
 Timing Scattered across days Starts after a change or an outage 
 Retry Works with another card Fails with every card 
 Order status Failed with a clear reason Pending payment although the gateway shows success 
 Gateway dashboard Decline logged with an issuer reason Errors logged, or no record of the attempt at all 
 
 How to fix it
 Re-enter and verify keys in the right mode, and re-register webhooks. Allow the gateway through your firewall rules. Update or replace the conflicting plugin.
 Loosen fraud rules that block genuine buyers. Keep API keys out of emails and chat messages. If your setup involves several gateways or custom rules, WooCommerce payment gateway integration help is available.


 

 
 NIGHTMARE 5 OF 5 · STOCK AND ORDERS
 Nightmare 5: How do inventory and integration errors create wrong orders?
 Because two systems disagree and the website is the one making the promise. When your store, warehouse system, marketplace or ERP hold different numbers, shoppers are sold items you do not have. They can also be charged shipping that does not match reality.
 What the customer sees
 An in-stock item followed by a sorry, it sold out email. The wrong variant arriving. A shipping cost that looks off, a delivery date that slips, or no tracking number after the order.
 Why it matters
 These failures happen after payment, so they cost more than a lost sale. The costs include refunds, support time, a customer who does not come back and sometimes a public review.
 Likely causes
 Slow sync: stock updated nightly or every few hours, so fast sellers oversell in between.
 Silent failures: a sync job fails, nobody is alerted, and the numbers drift for weeks.
 Several channels selling the same stock with nothing reserved when an order arrives.
 Mismatched SKUs or variation mapping between systems.
 Orders that never reach the warehouse or ERP because a field is missing or an API limit is hit.
 Out-of-date shipping data, such as missing weights or old rate tables.
 How to confirm it
 Pick ten best-selling products and compare stock in every system on the same day. Check the website, the warehouse or ERP, and any marketplace.
 Find the last successful sync and read its log. If your integration uses scheduled tasks, WooCommerce, then Status, then Scheduled Actions shows failed or overdue jobs.
 Take your last five oversold or wrong orders and trace each one. Note when it was placed, what stock the site showed, and what the other system said at that moment.
 Send a test order all the way through to the warehouse or ERP. Check the label, tracking number and customer email.
 Read support emails for phrases like out of stock after I paid or wrong item. They show patterns your reports miss.
 How to fix it
 Move fast-selling items from scheduled sync to near real-time sync. Pick one system as the source of truth. Keep a small safety buffer on scarce items.
 Set alerts for failed sync jobs and reconcile counts weekly. Clean up SKU mapping before you change anything else.
 When to bring in professional help
 Get help when three or more systems are involved. Custom integrations and middleware call for help too. So do logs that show errors you cannot interpret.
 Help is also worth getting when a fix would change how orders flow to the warehouse. ERP, warehouse and marketplace connections fall under ecommerce integration services . WooCommerce stores that mainly need accurate counts across channels can look at WooCommerce stock management plugin options .


 

 
 How do you find out which nightmare is costing you the most?
 Every horror story has a moment when someone finally turns the lights on. This is that moment for your store. Follow the money in order.
 Check where shoppers drop off, then check the technical reports for that step. Thirty minutes is enough to point you at the right nightmare.
 Open your funnel in GA4 and note the biggest drop between product view, cart, checkout and purchase, split by device.
 If the drop happens before checkout, run the speed and mobile checks from Nightmares 2 and 3.
 If the drop happens at checkout, test with three addresses and read the console, as in Nightmare 1.
 If shoppers reach payment and fail, review failed orders and gateway logs, as in Nightmare 4.
 If sales complete but customers complain afterwards, audit stock and sync, as in Nightmare 5.
 Repeat this monthly and after any plugin, theme or gateway change, since most of these problems start with a change. If the same problems keep returning, the platform or theme may be the cause. Weigh that with ecommerce website redesign warning signs , which help you judge whether to keep patching.
 Heading into the holiday rush? Run this triage first. Then work through the WooCommerce holiday season checklist .

 People also ask
 Why do shoppers abandon an online store at checkout?
 Shoppers leave when checkout breaks, slows down, or surprises them. A script error, a missing shipping rate, or a rejected field can stop a sale outright. Most shoppers never report it. They simply leave.
 How can you tell a payment failure from a normal decline?
 A technical failure hits many customers at once and often shows an error from your own setup. It tends to start right after a change. A normal decline is a single bank reason on a single order.
 How often should you test your store checkout?
 Test it monthly and after any plugin, theme or gateway change. Use a guest order on a real phone. Check the order, the email and the payment record each time.
 When is a slow store a sign you need more than quick fixes?
 Quick fixes work when a few heavy images or old tags cause the delay. If the same problems keep returning, the platform or theme may be the cause. That is the point to weigh a redesign instead of more patching.


 

 
 Conclusion
 Most of these nightmares are not mysteries. Each one leaves clues in places you can already reach. Examples are a browser console, an order note, a gateway dashboard and a stock comparison.
 Look at the step where shoppers drop off. Confirm the cause before you change anything. Fix one thing at a time so you can tell what worked.
 The best time to find a broken checkout is before a customer does. Place one test order today, on a phone, as a guest. Halloween ends on October 31, but a broken checkout will still be there on November 1 unless someone fixes it.


 

 
 Frequently Asked Questions

 

 
 How often should I test my checkout? 
 Place one real test order at least weekly, and again after every plugin, theme, gateway or hosting change. Use a different device and address each time so you do not keep testing the same path.


 Is it safe to troubleshoot on my live store? 
 Reading logs, order notes and reports is safe. Turning plugins off, changing settings or testing code is not, because shoppers are using the store while you do it. Use a staging copy for anything that changes behaviour, and take a full backup first.


 What should I send a developer when I report a checkout or payment bug? 
 Send the page address, the device and browser, and the time it happened. Add the order number if there is one and the exact message shown. Include a screenshot of the browser console if you can capture it.
 Steps to repeat the problem matter most. Never include API keys or passwords in the message.


 How can I find out about these problems before customers tell me? 
 Set up uptime monitoring and an alert for failed orders and stalled payments. Add a daily look at the gateway dashboard and a conversion-drop alert in your analytics. Keep a recurring test order on your calendar too.


 Do these problems affect SEO as well as sales? 
 Slow pages can, since page experience is one of many signals Google considers. Checkout, payment and stock problems do not affect rankings directly, but they waste the traffic you worked to earn.


 Are hosted platforms like Shopify free of these problems? 
 They remove some, such as server setup and plugin conflicts on the core store, but not all. Payment configuration, third-party apps, mobile design and integrations with your warehouse or ERP can still cause every nightmare here.
